claude.country: USA (multi-country datasets: ISIC from MSKCC and international centers; malaria from multiple countries incl. Myanmar; mPower)
claude.sample_unit: patients/samples across three datasets (1081 dermoscopy images; 1034 transcriptomic samples; 2804 participants)
models_evaluated: OOD detectors: isolation forest, KNN, class Mahalanobis, maximum softmax probability

links.outcome: Model AUROC on ID versus OOD subsets flagged by OOD detectors before model processing
links.effect: KNN OOD detector had mean ID-OOD AUROC differences of 0.256 on ISIC and 0.249 on malaria (p<0.05); several detectors, but not all, identified low-reliability subsets. Not consistent across detectors or age subgroups.
links.quote: These results indicate that this method can identify test observations associated with low classifier reliability on these datasets.

links.outcome: Model performance on test data differing from training distribution (new site, age, subgroup)
links.effect: OOD AUROC often fell below 0.5 for some detectors, showing subpopulations where the classifier was worse than random despite acceptable global performance.
links.quote: This highlights the importance of outlier detection in clinical classification applications where, even though the global performance of a classifier can be acceptable, there still can exist subpopulations for whom the classifier fails.

links.outcome: Model performance differences across demographic/clinical subgroups hidden by aggregate results
links.effect: Model performed worse in patients >75 on ISIC, in 10-16 hpi malaria samples, and in DBS Parkinson's patients; OOD detector benefit absent in patients >55 on ISIC.
links.quote: On these patients who had DBS, the model performed notably worse than on patients who did not have DBS (Figure 5c ).

unlisted_practices: Out-of-distribution detection ensembles of multiple detectors to reduce OOD flagging
Using OOD detection to identify underrepresented subgroups in training data

openai.country: Multiple; USA, Australia, Spain, Austria, Myanmar, and other countries not specified

links.effect: CE+KNN detected 6.8%-31.5% as OOD; ID-OOD AUROC differences were 0.256 (ISIC) and 0.249 (malaria), p < 0.05; not necessarily Parkinson's.
links.quote: We find that several, but not all, OOD detectors are able to identify patient subpopulations on which the model performs poorly or has higher variance (Figures 2 and 3 ), though these results were not always consistent across demographic groups (Table S3 ).

links.effect: OOD AUROC often fell below 0.5, indicating some test subpopulations were worse than random despite acceptable global performance.
links.quote: Indeed, for a few of the OOD detectors, the OOD AUROC often fell below 0.5, indicating that these algorithms found test observation sub‐populations where the clinical classifier was on average worse than random.

links.outcome: Performance in age and clinical subgroups
links.effect: Patients >75 performed worse than under 75; 10 to 16 HPI samples were slightly lower; DBS patients were notably worse; AUROCs not numerically reported in text.
links.quote: When we subset the test data to patients over 75, we found that the model had worse average performance on these patients compared to those under 75, in agreement with the OOD detector's predictions.

unlisted_practices: Ensembling OOD detectors by labeling observations OOD only when all detectors agree.

links.outcome: AUROC difference between in-distribution and out-of-distribution test subsets
links.effect: Mean AUROC difference between ID and OOD subsets was 0.256 on ISIC (p < 0.05) and 0.249 on malaria (p < 0.05); 6.8% to 31.5% of test data were detected as OOD.
links.quote: This method detected between 6.8% and 31.5% of the test dataset as being OOD, depending on the dataset, and had mean differences in AUROC between ID and OOD subsets of 0.256 on ISIC ( p < 0.05, two‐sided test for difference in means using the bootstrap distribution with Benjamini–Hochberg correction for multiple testing) and 0.249 on malaria ( p < 0.05; Figure 2a , Tables S1 and S2 ).

screen.practice: out-of-distribution detection to filter unreliable predictions
screen.reason: Empirically tests out-of-distribution (OOD) detection algorithms as a deployment safeguard/guardrail to filter out unreliable patient cases across three medical data modalities.
